profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is attributed to Prime, most likely Prime Data Centers given the California and Texas registry locations. Prime Data Centers own site states the company was established in 2017 in California and is now headquartered at 400 North Ervay Street, Dallas, Texas, under founder and CEO Nicholas Laag, and describes itself as majority founder owned. The company reports 28 data centers across 13 campuses globally with a 4 plus gigawatt expansion pipeline, and lists Silicon Valley and Dallas among its confirmed North America markets, alongside Austin, Chicago, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Sacramento, matching both states where this registry lists a Prime facility. No building specific address, opening date, or individual MW figures for this particular registry row were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
Prime DFW01-01 publishes 20 MW of IT capacity across 213,000 square feet of technical space in Dallas, with a power density that suggests mixed or general-purpose colocation rather than dense AI training clusters.

At 40 kW per rack, the published 20 MW supports roughly 500 racks; at 10 kW per rack, it supports roughly 2,000 racks. The operator has not published a target rack density, so which assumption applies remains unknown. The 94 watts per square foot working out from the published IT load ranks toward the lower end of AI-optimized facilities, implying the space may be sized for enterprise workloads across multiple use cases rather than concentrated GPU deployments. This inference depends on layout assumptions the operator has not disclosed.

SOC 2 Type 2 certification indicates the facility passed independent audit of security controls over a defined period, qualifying it for regulated enterprise workloads. ISO 27001 certification shows implementation of an audited information security management system. Neither certification speaks to power redundancy tier or cooling capacity, the infrastructure that determines whether this site can sustain the continuous demand AI training requires.

Within Texas, this facility ranks sixth among thirteen sites that have published a megawatt figure out of 133 total mapped facilities in the state. The thirteen published facilities account for 389 MW in aggregate; DFW01-01's 20 MW represents roughly 5 percent of that disclosed total. The remaining 120 mapped Texas facilities have published no capacity, so the 389 MW understates true state capacity by an unknown margin, and the sixth-place rank reflects only what operators chose to disclose rather than actual scale.
